passage: Coordinator's note, peer-listening circle, hostel common room, Thursday. Pairs practised talking about something recent. Sangeeta's partner, Ira, had just returned from her first solo trip to Shillong. Sangeeta began with "Did you like it?" Ira said, "Yeah, it was nice," and stopped. Sangeeta glanced at the prompt card, paused, and tried again: "What did it feel like, being there on your own?" Ira sat back. She described missing the bus on the first day, panicking at the stand, then eating momos with a stranger's family who helped her find the right route. She laughed while telling it and said she had not told anyone that part. The whole answer took nearly four minutes, against four seconds for the first. Afterwards Sangeeta told the group that the first question already had its answer tucked inside it. Next session I will ask every pair to swap one yes-or-no question for a "how" question and notice what changes.

qa.q: Where had Ira just returned from?
qa.a: Ira had just returned from her first solo trip to Shillong.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta pause and try a second question?
qa.a: Sangeeta seemed a little uneasy that "it was nice" had ended the talk so fast, and curious to hear more, so she tried a question that could not be answered with a yes.

qa.q: What small step does the coordinator plan for the next session?
qa.a: Every pair will swap one yes-or-no question for a "how" question and notice what changes, which is a simple, kind way to practise 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Ira when the second question came?
qa.a: Ira got room to tell the real story, the panic at the bus stand and the kind strangers, instead of just agreeing that the trip was nice.

grounding: Shows a young adult swapping a closed "did you like it" question for an open question about how the trip felt and getting a much fuller story.

passage: I'm Vinita, and last month I sent a bank-holiday notice to the wrong mailing list. Nirmala called me into the glass cabin before I had even sat down. "Why would you send it? What was going on in your head? Who approved it? Did you even check?" Each question landed before I had finished answering the last. My mind went blank. I kept saying "I don't know", which was not even true. I just felt cornered. Two days later Nirmala came to my desk with two cups of tea. "I came at you too fast on Monday," she said. "Can you walk me through what the send looked like from your side?" Almost the same questions, really. But this time I remembered the filter that had reset overnight, the rushed deadline, the second check nobody did. We fixed the filter together in twenty minutes. Looking back, I had the answers all along. I just couldn't reach them while I was busy defending myself.

qa.q: What had reset overnight?
qa.a: The filter had reset overnight.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling during the quick questions in the glass cabin?
qa.a: Vinita felt attacked and cornered; the mind went blank and "I don't know" came out even though it was not true.

qa.q: What could Nirmala try the next time a mistake happens on the team?
qa.a: Ask one calm question at a time, like "walk me through it from your side", and wait for the whole answer before asking the next.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see the Monday meeting two days later?
qa.a: Nirmala seems to see that the rapid-fire questions got only "I don't know", and that a gentler tone was what finally brought out the real causes.

grounding: Shows a person who goes blank under quick, attacking questions and then gives full answers when the same questions come with a softer tone and real curiosity.

passage: The deck was due to the client at six, and it was already 4:40 when the office power flickered and the backup generator kicked in with a hum. Tejas scrolled fast through the slides: new delivery routes for a bakery chain, three depots, every order dropped by seven the next morning. "Looks done," he said, reaching to send it. Charu held up a hand. "Give me two minutes. What could break this on day one?" Tejas sighed and glanced at the clock. "Nothing. The numbers work." "Then what am I missing? You drove these routes last year." He stopped scrolling. "Actually... the Hosur depot road floods every monsoon. We'd miss the seven o'clock drop for weeks." They added one slide with a backup route and a line about rain delays. At 5:52 the deck went out. The next morning the client's operations head replied that the monsoon slide was the first one she had read closely.

qa.q: At what time did the deck go out?
qa.a: At 5:52 the deck went out.

qa.q: Why did Charu ask "what am I missing" despite the rush?
qa.a: Charu seemed calm but uneasy that a plan checked in a hurry might hide a risk, and respected that Tejas knew the routes better from driving them.

qa.q: What small habit could the team keep from this evening?
qa.a: Before sending any plan, spend two minutes asking what would make it fail, and ask whoever knows the ground best what they see.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about the question once he remembered the flooding road?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved that the flaw surfaced before sending, and a little valued, because the question was asked on the strength of his own experience.

grounding: Shows Charu, under time pressure, asking what could break a plan and what is being missed, which surfaces a hidden risk and draws on the other person's knowledge.

passage:
Monday: Tanuja wails when her block tower falls. Vijay kneels, rebuilds it fast, shows her the new top. She keeps crying.
Wednesday: she howls at bath time, and nobody can tell why. Vijay lifts her, holds her close, hums softly. Her sobs slow. Her cheek rests on his shoulder.
Saturday: she trips on the rug and cries. This time she toddles straight to Vijay, arms up, and settles as soon as he holds her and murmurs, "I'm here."

qa.q: What does Vijay do on Wednesday when Tanuja howls at bath time?
qa.a: Vijay lifts her, holds her close, hums softly.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's cheek resting on Vijay's shoulder suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels safe and calmer, comforted by being held even though nobody found out what was wrong 🙂

qa.q: What could a caregiver try when a toddler cries and the reason is unclear?
qa.a: Pick the child up, hold them close and speak or hum softly first, before trying to work out or fix the cause.

qa.q: What changed for Vijay between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday Vijay tried to fix the tower and the crying went on; by Saturday Tanuja reached for Vijay's arms, so Vijay could comfort her without knowing the cause.

grounding: Shows a crying toddler who quiets when held and spoken to softly, whatever the cause, across three different days.

passage: At the daycare gate, Tarun would not put his shoes on. He kicked one across the mat and pressed his face into his cubby. Minakshi crouched beside him. The teacher whispered that Isha's family was moving to another city, and today was her last day. Minakshi rubbed his back. "You are sad because Isha left," she said quietly. "You wanted to play with her tomorrow too." Tarun lifted his face and nodded. His lip wobbled, then stopped. He fetched the kicked shoe himself. "Mumma, can we draw her a picture?" he asked.

qa.q: Why was it Isha's last day?
qa.a: Isha's family was moving to another city.

qa.q: How can you tell Tarun felt calmer after Minakshi spoke?
qa.a: He lifted his face and nodded, his lip stopped wobbling and he fetched the shoe himself, so he felt understood and less upset.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do next to help Tarun?
qa.a: She could say yes to drawing Isha a picture together, which gives his sadness something gentle to do.

qa.q: Why might the teacher's whisper matter to Minakshi?
qa.a: Without it, Minakshi might have seen only a child refusing his shoes; knowing about Isha let her name the real feeling instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a parent naming a small child's sadness about a friend leaving, and the child nodding and calming.

passage: The final whistle went on the muddy pitch behind the leisure centre in Leeds, and Alejandro's team had lost four to three. He had missed the last penalty. He sat on the bench, shoulders shaking, tears mixing with the drizzle. Coach Chidi walked past with the ball bag. "Come on, it's only a game. Enough crying." Two boys snickered. Alejandro scrubbed his face hard with his sleeve and stared at his boots. In the car his mum asked how it went. "Fine," he said. That night he lay awake replaying the ball skimming past the post, and told no one. The next Saturday he scraped his knee badly in training, bit his lip, and said it didn't hurt.

qa.q: What was the final score?
qa.a: Alejandro's team had lost four to three.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro say "Fine" in the car?
qa.a: He still felt hurt and ashamed about the missed penalty, but after being told to stop crying he was hiding it rather than risk being mocked again.

qa.q: What could a coach say to a child crying after a loss?
qa.a: Something like "That penalty really stings, doesn't it?" while sitting beside him for a minute, before any talk about next time.

qa.q: What would change if Coach Chidi had sat down beside Alejandro instead?
qa.a: Alejandro might have cried a bit longer and then told someone about the penalty, learning that big feelings are allowed instead of something to hide.

grounding: Shows a child told that a lost match is just a game and to stop crying, who then learns to hide feelings rather than stop having them.

subtype: Wanting to be heard, not advised [Receiver]
passage:
Sabina didi,
I'm writing this because on a call it would come out wrong.
Remember last Tuesday, when I rang you after Kulkarni sir read my history essay aloud as an example of "what not to do"? I'd barely finished the story when you said: talk to him after class, rewrite it tonight, ask for the marking scheme, email the class teacher, maybe join a writing club.
All good ideas, probably. But I went quiet and said I had homework.
That's also why I didn't tell you about the cricket selection.
I don't need a plan the second I start talking. I need you to say "ugh, that's so unfair" and let me be annoyed for five minutes. If I want ideas, I'll ask. Promise.
You're still the first person I want to call.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Kulkarni sir read aloud?
qa.a: He read Darshan's history essay aloud as an example of "what not to do".

qa.q: Why did Darshan go quiet and mention homework on that call?
qa.a: Darshan felt unheard and deflated when five fixes came before any sympathy, so ending the call seemed easier than explaining.

qa.q: What could Sabina say the next time Darshan calls upset?
qa.a: She could start with "that sounds so unfair", let Darshan vent, and then ask whether Darshan wants ideas or just to rant.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sabina might feel stung at first, since the ideas were meant kindly, then relieved to understand the silence and touched to still be the first person Darshan wants to call.

grounding: Shows a teenager who stopped sharing after a vent about a teacher was answered with a string of solutions, asking to be heard first.

passage: Binita, sit. Moushumi hung up on you after you sent her three job links? Let me tell you something from when your Nani Salma was twenty-five and working night shifts at the district hospital. My friend Rehana came into the nurses' room one evening, eyes swollen. Her engagement had been called off that morning. My first instinct was to start fixing: talk to his mother, find another match, take leave. But I saw her face. So I only said, "That sounds really hard, Rehana." She nodded and cried properly then. After a while I asked, "Do you want ideas, or just company tonight?" "Company," she said. So I shared my tea and my stool until her bus came at eleven. Two weeks later she came back and said, "Now tell me your ideas." And she listened to every one, because this time she had asked for them.

qa.q: Where was Salma working when Rehana came into the nurses' room?
qa.a: Salma was working night shifts at the district hospital.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when her first instinct was to start fixing?
qa.a: Salma felt worried for Rehana and eager to help, but seeing her face made Salma hold back the fixes and stay with the sadness first.

qa.q: Which choice in the nurses' room worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying "That sounds really hard" and then asking "ideas or just company?" worked, because Rehana could cry freely and decide for herself when she wanted advice.

qa.q: What was it like for Rehana when Salma asked instead of advising?
qa.a: Rehana could grieve the called-off engagement without pressure, and two weeks later she felt ready and asked for the ideas herself.

grounding: Shows someone who first says a situation sounds hard and then asks whether the friend wants ideas or just company, respecting both feeling and choice.

passage: Behind the chapel in the village, Maria and Farida crouched over hopscotch squares scratched in the red dirt. "Your foot touched the line! Out!" Maria shouted. "It did not!" "It did!" "Did NOT!" Each time Maria said it louder, Farida said it louder back, until a goat trotted away. Jude, mending a fishing net nearby, called, "Maria, before you answer, say what Farida just said." Maria scowled. "She says... her heel was on the line but her toes were inside." She stopped. That was different from what she had been fighting about. "So only your heel?" Farida nodded, still frowning. They had never decided what counts. Heels count, they agreed, and Farida hopped again, carefully.

qa.q: Where were the hopscotch squares?
qa.a: They were scratched in the red dirt behind the chapel in the village.

qa.q: Why did Maria scowl when Jude spoke up?
qa.a: Maria felt annoyed at being stopped mid-argument and still wanted to win, so saying Farida's side out loud felt like giving in.

qa.q: What could the two try the next time a game argument starts?
qa.a: Each could say back the other's point first, like "you mean only your heel?", and then agree on a rule together.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt once Maria repeated her point?
qa.a: Farida likely felt heard for the first time in the quarrel, which let her calm down enough to agree on a rule, though she was still a bit cross.

grounding: Shows children shouting the same claim louder over a game until one of them says back what the other said, which starts to change the pattern.

passage: In the Lajpat Nagar flat, Pema's phone blinked at four percent and the charger was missing from the socket again. She found it plugged in beside Sabina's bed. "You always take my stuff! You never ask! Just like my jacket last Diwali, and the time you read my diary—" "Always?" Sabina shot up. "I asked you on Sunday. And the diary was three years ago, Pema!" Within a minute they were shouting about who had got the window seat on every trip since Class 5. Pema stormed out to the balcony. From there she heard Sabina's voice go thick, the way it did when she was hurt. The online class started at six. Pema came back in, slower. "Okay. Not always. Today I need the charger back before six, and can you ask before you take it?" Sabina unplugged it without a word, then said, "Fine. I'll ask."

qa.q: How much charge was left on Pema's phone?
qa.a: Pema's phone blinked at four percent.

qa.q: What might Pema have felt on the balcony when Sabina's voice went thick?
qa.a: Pema probably felt a pang of guilt as the anger cooled, sensing that dragging in old grievances had hurt Sabina.

qa.q: What made Pema's second try work?
qa.a: Naming one present problem, the charger before six, and one request, to ask first, gave Sabina something she could agree to instead of something to defend against.

qa.q: How did Pema's "always" and "never" sound to Sabina?
qa.a: They sounded unfair and like an attack, since Sabina had asked on Sunday, so she defended herself and the fight spread to old seat quarrels.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose "always" and "never" plus old grievances escalate a quarrel, and who then gets somewhere by naming the specific problem of today.
